edits.reason: Bonding predicts tendencies, not universal electrical properties.
edits.before: - **Nothing?** → it's an insulator and brittle
edits.after: - **No easy charge transport or slip?** → expect low electrical conductivity and brittle behaviour; check exceptions such as semiconductors.

edits.reason: SiC is a semiconductor, not a categorical insulator.
edits.before: | **nothing** | insulator, **brittle**, very high melting point | diamond, silicon carbide |
edits.after: | little easy slip | often insulating or semiconducting, **brittle**, high-temperature resistance | diamond, silicon carbide |

edits.reason: Distinguish Coulomb energy, force and strength.
edits.before: Strength depends on **charge × charge ÷ distance**.
edits.after: The attractive **energy** scales with charge × charge ÷ distance; the attractive **force** scales with charge × charge ÷ distance². Neither alone is a bulk-strength formula.

edits.reason: Introduce looked-up material value before use.
edits.before: - Double charges, tightly packed → **melts near 2,850 °C**
edits.after: - Double charges, tightly packed → predict a **high melting temperature**; **about 2,850 °C is a supplied reference value**, not a result calculated from the bond.

edits.reason: Do not imply bonding gives an exact melting temperature.
edits.before: All of this was predicted from the bond, before looking anything up.
edits.after: The qualitative property package follows from the bonding. The numerical melting temperature must be looked up.

edits.reason: No universal warning before tool failure.

edits.after: **Many ductile steel parts bend** before breaking; hardened or embrittled tools may fracture without that warning

edits.after: sheets slide off easily; conducts much less well across the layers

edits.reason: Clarify causal order while retaining the four linked topics.

edits.reason: Avoid predicting insulation from covalent bonding alone.

edits.reason: Record a prediction correction instead of asserting every prediction was right.
edits.before: Silicon carbide is the grit on grinding wheels and sandpaper, and it matches every prediction.
edits.after: Silicon carbide is used as abrasive grit and is a semiconductor. The mechanical predictions fit; the electrical exception is a reason to check rather than trust the bond label alone.

edits.reason: Direction-dependent is not on/off.

edits.reason: Avoid deterministic failure claims from a family label.

edits.after: A brittle ceramic may need a different geometry, support or impact rating. Bonding alone cannot certify whether an impact will break it.

edits.after: | **HCP** (hexagonal close-packed) | hexagonal stacking | **6** in the conventional hexagonal cell (2 in a primitive cell) |

edits.before: It's also why the Titanic's steel cracked in icy water.
edits.after: Cold-service toughness also depends on grade, processing, flaws, loading rate and section thickness; crystal structure alone is not a failure diagnosis.

edits.before: it **can't continue**

edits.reason: Amorphous solids retain short-range order.
edits.before: solids with **no pattern at all**
edits.after: solids with **no long-range repeating pattern**

edits.reason: Distinguish glass transition, rubbery behaviour and melting.
edits.before: Above it, the material flows like extremely thick syrup.
edits.after: Above it, the amorphous regions become more mobile and often rubbery; this is not automatically melting or free flow. Crystals and crosslinks can still support the material.

edits.reason: Separate glass-fracture features from cleavage river patterns.
edits.before: | **Mirror-smooth with "river" lines** | glass or a glassy material |
edits.after: | **Mirror, mist and hackle regions** | often glass fracture; river patterns are commonly associated with crystalline cleavage |

edits.reason: Replace blanket material prohibition with a property check.
edits.before: Never use it where you need warning.
edits.after: Check the specific alloy, geometry and failure behaviour where warning before failure matters.

edits.reason: Work hardening raises strength, not Young's modulus.
edits.before: gets **stiffer** (cold work, tangled dislocations)
edits.after: gets **harder to bend permanently** (cold work, tangled dislocations), without a comparable increase in elastic modulus

edits.reason: Keep explanation distinct from a repair procedure.
edits.before: Heat it with a torch and let it cool, and it's **soft** again (annealed).
edits.after: A controlled anneal can restore ductility. For a real component, follow the alloy and component specification rather than treating this as a torch-heating procedure.

edits.reason: Carbon in iron diffuses interstitially.
edits.before: They hop from vacancy to vacancy (lesson 7), moving from **crowded to less crowded**.
edits.after: Substitutional atoms can hop into vacancies; small atoms such as carbon in iron move between interstitial sites. In this simple concentration-driven model, the net flow goes from **higher to lower concentration**.

edits.reason: Define flux including its area denominator.
edits.before: - **J** = how many atoms flow through per second
edits.after: - **J** = diffusion flux: amount crossing **unit area per second** (for example atoms/(m²·s), with a compatible concentration scale)

edits.reason: Annealing outcome depends on alloy and treatment.
edits.before: Result: **soft, ductile, stress-free**.
edits.after: Result: usually **softer and more ductile**, with reduced residual stress—not a guarantee of zero stress.

edits.reason: Do not treat TTT as a literal continuous-cooling schedule.
edits.before: To get martensite, you must cool **past the nose** before it has time to transform into softer structures.
edits.after: A TTT chart describes isothermal holds; a continuous-cooling transformation (CCT) chart is the appropriate map for a changing cooling path. The teaching idea is to avoid substantial diffusional transformation before reaching the martensite range.

edits.reason: Explain the load decrease rather than a denominator-only bookkeeping effect.
edits.before: The bar is necking. The real area at the neck is shrinking, but engineering stress still divides by the **original** area, so the curve dips even though the material at the neck is still getting stronger.
edits.after: After necking, the measured load falls while engineering stress still divides by the fixed **original** area. Local true stress may continue rising as the neck thins; damage can later reverse that trend.

edits.reason: Tensile toughness alone is not an impact certification.
edits.before: The high-strength bar snaps first when hit.
edits.after: For these illustrative curves and equal material volume, the high-strength bar has the lower tensile energy capacity. A real impact also depends on geometry, notches, loading rate and temperature.

edits.reason: Remove unsupported universal measurement accuracy.
edits.before: Even done well, expect about **1% error on E** and **a few % on yield**. That's the method's normal error, not a mistake.
edits.after: Use the test method, instrument calibration and specimen repeatability to estimate uncertainty; a universal 1% error cannot be promised.

edits.reason: Do not misdescribe engineering stress after necking.
edits.before: The fall after necking is a bookkeeping effect.
edits.after: The fall in engineering stress reflects a falling measured load, using a fixed original area.

edits.reason: Bound the stress convention to the model.
edits.before: **For design, use engineering stress.** Your part's cross-section is the original one.
edits.after: **For these small-deformation classroom checks, use engineering stress** with compatible allowables. Large-deformation models may require true stress and strain.

edits.reason: A three-specimen estimate is not a certified allowable.
edits.before: **Mean − 2s** is a quick screen: most bars will be stronger than that. (Real certified aerospace values need many more test bars and extra statistics.)
edits.after: **Mean − 2s is only a classroom screening estimate.** With three specimens it does not establish a certified lower bound or a stated population coverage. Real allowables need the applicable sampling and tolerance-bound method.

edits.after: **Supplied classroom model for 1045 steel:** σ₀ = 110 MPa, k = **0.65 MPa·√m**, with d entered in metres:

edits.reason: Distinguish work hardening from stiffness.
edits.before: Bend a wire back and forth: it gets stiffer each time, then snaps.
edits.after: Bend a wire back and forth: it resists further permanent bending more strongly, but accumulating damage can make it crack. Elastic stiffness is a different property.

edits.reason: Not an absolute block of every dislocation.
edits.before: That distortion **blocks every dislocation**.
edits.after: That distortion and the resulting microstructure strongly impede dislocation motion.

edits.reason: T6 is a treatment designation, not an unconditional maximum-strength claim.
edits.before: **T6** = artificially aged to peak strength
edits.after: **T6** = solution heat-treated and artificially aged; the specified condition is alloy-dependent

edits.reason: Do not turn a geometry example into an unsafe repair instruction.
edits.before: - **Drill a small "stop hole"** at the tip of a crack. It turns an infinitely sharp tip into a rounded one, which can stop the crack running.
edits.after: - A rounded crack tip reduces an ideal elastic stress concentration, but **stop-drilling is not a general repair approval**. A cracked load-bearing part needs its specified inspection and repair or replacement process.

edits.reason: Detectability alone cannot establish safety.
edits.before: - a_c well above the detection limit → OK
edits.after: - a_c above the detection limit → a necessary first check, not approval; allow for detection probability, growth, inspection intervals and margin

edits.reason: Miner damage fraction is not a universal fraction of lifetime.
edits.before: Total = **0.75**, so a quarter of the life is left
edits.after: Total = **0.75**, so one quarter of this model's damage budget remains—not necessarily one quarter of the service time

edits.reason: Practice answer does not imply guaranteed remaining life.
edits.before: so about 39% of its life is left
edits.after: so about 39% of the model's damage budget remains; remaining cycles depend on the future loading

edits.reason: Avoid an infinite-life guarantee.
edits.before: Below that, it effectively lasts forever (the **endurance limit**).
edits.after: Some tested steels show an **endurance limit** under specified conditions; corrosion, welds, notches and variable loading can invalidate it.

edits.reason: Qualify fatigue screening.
edits.before: **Steel below its endurance limit** can last indefinitely. **Aluminium can't**, so plan inspections.
edits.after: Use a fatigue curve for the actual material, surface, environment and loading. An ideal endurance limit is not a maintenance exemption.

edits.reason: 13× is greater than the stated 10× threshold.

edits.after: roughly 13× the test time, so it exceeds this lesson's illustrative 10× caution threshold

edits.reason: Strain-limit time differs from rupture life.
edits.before: Work out how much stretch the part can tolerate, divide by the steady rate, and you have its life.
edits.after: Allowed creep strain divided by a representative steady rate estimates time to that strain limit. It does not by itself predict rupture life.

edits.reason: Match method to the corrected creep distinction.

edits.after: allowed strain ÷ rate = approximate time to the strain limit; check rupture separately

edits.reason: State the rule-of-mixtures model limit.
edits.before: **Across the fibres (series):** the load passes **through** fibre, then matrix, then fibre.
edits.after: **Across the fibres (series approximation):** imagine an ideal equal-stress arrangement of fibre and matrix. This gives a useful simple bound, not an exact transverse-modulus model for every composite.

8: Given: D₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, Q = 148,000 J/mol and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). The 0.80 mm diffusion length is not the same as the 0.69 mm depth to 0.4% carbon.
